label: raising capital and business acquisition
overview: Capital raising engagements span a wide spectrum — from a founder seeking their first equity investor to an experienced operator acquiring a business through a search fund model. The advisor's role is to match the client's specific capital requirement to the right vehicle and prepare them for the rigorous scrutiny of investors, lenders, or vendors. The critical diagnostic step is identifying which of the five capital pathways applies, as each has distinct preparation requirements, investor expectations, and risk profiles. Misjudging the pathway — for example, approaching venture capital investors with a lifestyle business pitch — wastes time and damages credibility.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the capital requirement driven by growth equity funding for an existing business, acquisition financing for purchasing another business, transformation capital for a major strategic change, a new venture launch, or a franchise or search fund model?
diagnostic_entry.growth_equity: The client has an established business with proven revenue and is seeking capital to accelerate growth. Focus on investor-ready financials, the pitch deck narrative, and equity dilution strategy. The investor's return expectation and exit timeline must be agreed before term sheet negotiation begins.
diagnostic_entry.acquisition_financing: The client is purchasing an existing business and needs to structure debt, equity, and vendor financing components. Due diligence quality, business valuation, and financing structure are the critical workstreams. Refer to the due-diligence domain for the DD framework.
diagnostic_entry.transformation_capital: The client needs capital to fund a significant operational or strategic transformation — new technology, market entry, business model shift. Focus on the strategic rationale, ROI model, and risk mitigation plan. Investors in transformation capital require a clear path to payback.
diagnostic_entry.new_venture: The client is launching a new business and needs seed or early-stage funding. Focus on MVP validation, total addressable market sizing, and the founder narrative. The pitch must demonstrate problem-solution fit before any financial projections are credible.
diagnostic_entry.search_fund_or_franchise: The client is using a structured acquisition vehicle — either a search fund (raising capital to search for and acquire an SME) or a franchise model (acquiring a proven operating system). Each has specific investor expectations around search criteria, acquisition thesis, and operator capability.

materials.name: Startup Pitch Deck
materials.summary: A slide-by-slide structure for pitching to investors that answers the critical questions concisely instead of burying them. It forces the founder to distil the business model, the competitive advantage and the financial need into something digestible, and gives the advisor a frame for walking them through their Status Quo, Problem and Solution until the narrative is investor-ready.
materials.who_when: Early-stage startups and entrepreneurs seeking seed capital, venture capital or angel investment.
steps: Executive summary — state exactly what funding is required, what it is for, the year-3 revenue and profit targets, and what makes the position unique.
Define the problem and solution — outline the global status quo, specify the local problem for each level of user, and present the solution's three main advantages.
Analyse market and competition — name the key competitors, explain why they fail to solve the problem, and state the single point of difference. Quantify the total potential market.
Detail the business model and traction — how the product is charged for (by the pack, by the box, store support) plus historical milestones and revenue achieved to date.
Make the Ask — present the target metrics for scaling and set out exactly how the money will be used, such as recruiting sales or production staff.

materials.name: Venture Capital Investment Cycle
materials.summary: Breaks the venture capital relationship into three phases — pre-investment, post-investment and exit — so a founder sees the whole arc rather than the raise alone. It removes the illusion of speed and prepares them for a long-term partnership, and it gives the advisor the ground for early conversations about valuation, control, and the exit that will eventually be expected.
materials.who_when: High-growth startups targeting institutional venture capital.
steps: Pre-investment — identify target investors by stage and industry, deliver a formal pitch, and negotiate the term sheet that sets valuation and control.
Post-investment — manage the relationship deliberately through consistent communication, mutual trust and established objectivity.
Exit — plan a timely and harmonious exit, whether an IPO or a sale, that aligns with the investor's return expectations rather than colliding with them.

materials.name: Six Procedural Hurdles of Fundraising
materials.summary: The six-month funnel a raise actually runs through, laid out so founders stop expecting money to change hands after one good meeting. Skipping a step is a common cause of failure. For the advisor it turns fundraising into a trackable pipeline with defined milestones rather than a series of hopeful conversations.
materials.who_when: Founders actively out in the market looking for funding.
steps: Warm introduction — secure a genuine first contact with the firm rather than a cold approach.
Pitch deck submission — send the formal business overview through.
Initial screen — a preliminary phone conversation to gauge whether there is real interest.
First meeting — a deep dive into the business model and, just as importantly, the team.
Second meeting — granular data such as lifetime value against customer acquisition cost, usually for a wider partner group or a technical review.
Deal structuring — approval of the fundraising documents and the transfer of cash.

materials.name: 90-Day Due Diligence Preparation Plan
materials.summary: Turns an overwhelming legal, financial and tax compliance burden into a chronological three-month project. Being investor-ready before a term sheet is signed builds confidence and shortens the close, and it gives the advisor a hard timeline for project-managing the internal clean-up — unassigned intellectual property and revenue mismatches being the usual offenders.
materials.who_when: Startups with a funding round three to six months away who know they have compliance gaps to close.
steps: Month 1, audit and assess — run an internal compliance health check, list pending statutory filings, review material contracts, and confirm IP ownership and assignment.
Month 2, organise and fix — reconcile financial statements against GST and bank records, execute the missing agreements such as founder vesting and IP assignment, and clear any pending tax notices.

Month 3, package and present — build the Virtual Data Room with its ten folders (Corporate, Cap Table, Financial, Tax, Legal, HR, IP, Tech, Commercial, Insurance), prepare the financial projections, and brief the customer references.

materials.name: Kotter's 8-Step Change Management Process
materials.summary: A pragmatic sequence for putting a strategic transformation into practice without it failing on execution. It carries leadership through the hard middle of a restructure and insists the new way is anchored in the culture rather than announced and abandoned — which is what separates a change that holds from one that quietly reverts.
materials.who_when: Established businesses implementing a major organisational change.
steps: Create a sense of urgency.
Build a guiding coalition.
Develop the vision and strategy.
Communicate the change vision.
Empower employees on a broad basis.
Generate quick wins.
Consolidate the gains and produce more change.
Anchor the new approaches in the corporate culture.

materials.name: Six Patterns of Entrepreneurship
materials.summary: Widens entrepreneurship beyond the Silicon Valley template so a founder can weigh risk, control and lifestyle against six real paths. Its central question is Rich versus Royal — maximum wealth or retained control — and answering it honestly points to the financing and operating structure that actually fits the life the client wants.
materials.who_when: Aspiring entrepreneurs, MBA graduates, and family business successors.
steps: Evaluate lifestyle and control goals — the desire for substantial wealth (Rich) against the desire to keep decision-making control (Royal).
Select the pattern — VC-backed technology, cool branded consumer products, boring and basic operations, a franchisee model, a search fund acquisition, or a family business takeover.
Align capital and risk to the choice — VC funding carries high risk and costs control, while bootstrapping, debt finance or a search fund keeps far more of it.

advisor_guidance.pathway_first: Identifying which of the five capital pathways applies is the most important step in any capital raising engagement. Applying VC pitch preparation to a franchise acquisition or a search fund pitch wastes the client's time and credibility. Spend the first meeting establishing which pathway is correct before any other work begins.
advisor_guidance.investors_fund_people: Across all five pathways, the quality of the operator is evaluated as critically as the financial model. A strong business case with a weak founder narrative will not close capital. Coach the client's story — their domain expertise, their track record, why they are uniquely qualified to execute — before reviewing the financial slides.
advisor_guidance.term_sheets_are_not_standard: Clients frequently assume that term sheets are largely standardised and the only negotiable item is valuation. The most economically significant terms are often buried in the liquidation preference and anti-dilution provisions. Always model the economics of the term sheet across multiple exit scenarios before advising the client to accept or reject.
advisor_guidance.acquisition_due_diligence_is_not_optiona: For any capital raise funding a business acquisition, the quality of the due diligence determines the quality of the purchase decision. Refer to the due-diligence domain framework and insist on independent legal, financial, and operational DD regardless of time pressure from the vendor.
